title: Large Blob Handling System Design Quiz

questions.question: Range requests enable resumable downloads for large files.

questionData.question: Range requests enable resumable downloads for large files.

questions.explanation: HTTP range requests let clients download specific byte ranges, enabling resumable downloads when connections fail partway through large files.

questions.question: Why would you use a signed CDN URL instead of a plain public URL for downloads?

options: It compresses the file during transfer
It grants time-limited, authorized access to content served from edge caches
It guarantees the file has been scanned for malware
It permanently caches the file on the client device
questionData.question: Why would you use a signed CDN URL instead of a plain public URL for downloads?

questions.explanation: A signed CDN URL lets you serve private content from edge caches while still controlling who can access it and for how long. The signature encodes an expiry and scope, so a leaked link stops working once it expires.

questions.question: What should you include in presigned URLs to prevent abuse?

options: User's IP address embedded in the URL signature for origin verification
Content-length-range and content-type restrictions
Database transaction ID
CDN cache headers
questionData.question: What should you include in presigned URLs to prevent abuse?

questions.explanation: Restrictions like content-length-range and content-type are baked into the signature, preventing users from uploading unexpected file sizes or types.

questions.question: A client uses S3 multipart upload and loses its connection after some parts succeed. Order these selected steps from setup through completion.

items: The client starts uploading parts and records the checksum returned for each part that succeeds
After reconnecting, the client uses the upload ID to ask S3 which parts succeeded, then uploads only the missing ones
Once all parts have uploaded, the client sends the part numbers and checksums to the completion endpoint, and S3 assembles the object
The client splits the file into parts of at least 5 MB, starts a multipart upload to get an upload ID, and gets a presigned URL for each part
questionData.question: A client uses S3 multipart upload and loses its connection after some parts succeed. Order these selected steps from setup through completion.

questions.explanation: The client first creates the multipart upload and gets the upload ID and presigned part URLs, then uploads parts while recording their checksums. After reconnecting, it uses the upload ID with ListParts to find the missing parts instead of starting over. Once every part is in, it calls the completion endpoint so S3 assembles the final object.

questions.question: You are serving private files that are downloaded rarely, and you want the simplest low-cost approach. Which download strategy best fits the article’s guidance?

options: Use a signed CDN URL because CDNs are always cheaper than blob storage.
Use a signed blob storage URL because direct blob access is simpler and cheaper for infrequent downloads.
Proxy every download through the application server so the server can stream the bytes.
Store the file contents in the database so downloads can use normal SQL queries.
questionData.question: You are serving private files that are downloaded rarely, and you want the simplest low-cost approach. Which download strategy best fits the article’s guidance?

questions.explanation: The article distinguishes direct blob storage downloads from CDN delivery. Direct blob storage access is simpler and cheaper for infrequent downloads, while a CDN is worth the extra cost when files are frequently accessed and benefit from caching and geographic distribution.

questions.question: A user starts a multipart upload but closes their laptop before the upload is completed. What should the system do to avoid wasting storage cost?

options: Use lifecycle rules to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a short period, because uploaded parts can remain stored and billable without forming an accessible file.
Immediately mark the file as completed in the database, because some parts have already reached blob storage.
Keep the partial upload forever, because incomplete multipart uploads are automatically free.
Ask the CDN to delete the partial chunks, because CDN edge servers own multipart upload state.
questionData.question: A user starts a multipart upload but closes their laptop before the upload is completed. What should the system do to avoid wasting storage cost?

questions.explanation: In multipart uploads, parts may exist in storage before the final completion call assembles them into a single object. Until completion succeeds there is no accessible final file, but the incomplete parts can still cost money, so lifecycle cleanup after 24–48 hours is recommended.

questions.question: When choosing a part size for a multipart upload, what is the main downside of using very small parts?

options: Smaller parts reduce total upload bandwidth
More parts mean more requests and more per-request overhead
Smaller parts cannot be retried independently
Smaller parts require proxying the upload through your servers
questionData.question: When choosing a part size for a multipart upload, what is the main downside of using very small parts?

questions.explanation: Smaller parts give finer-grained retries but multiply the number of upload requests, adding round-trip and per-request overhead. Larger parts cut that overhead but waste more work when a single part fails and has to be re-uploaded.

questions.question: A compliance requirement says you must scan every uploaded file for malware BEFORE the file is accessible to other users. Which approach works with direct uploads?

options: Proxy all uploads through your servers for inline scanning
Upload to quarantine first, scan, then move to the public location
Add malware scanning headers to the presigned URL
Direct uploads cannot support any form of malware scanning
questionData.question: A compliance requirement says you must scan every uploaded file for malware BEFORE the file is accessible to other users. Which approach works with direct uploads?

questions.explanation: With direct uploads, you can use a quarantine bucket pattern: files are uploaded directly to a quarantine location, then a serverless function or worker scans them and moves clean files to the public location. This preserves the performance benefits of direct uploads while meeting compliance requirements.

questions.question: How do cloud storage services help with state synchronization?

options: Automatic database updates via built-in ORM integrations
Event notifications when files are uploaded
Real-time replication
Built-in caching
questionData.question: How do cloud storage services help with state synchronization?

questions.explanation: Storage services publish events (S3 to SNS/SQS, GCS to Pub/Sub) when files are uploaded, letting your system update database status reliably.

questions.question: What is the primary problem with proxying large files through application servers?

options: Security vulnerabilities from handling raw file bytes
Application servers become bottlenecks with no added value
Increased storage costs
Database performance degradation
questionData.question: What is the primary problem with proxying large files through application servers?

questions.explanation: Application servers add latency and consume resources without adding value to the file transfer, creating unnecessary bottlenecks when files could go directly to blob storage.

questions.question: In an S3-style multipart upload, the client successfully uploads every part but crashes before calling the completion endpoint. What is the correct system behavior to design for?

options: The object is immediately readable because all bytes have reached blob storage.
No final object is readable yet; the uploaded parts remain as incomplete multipart state and should be cleaned up by abort/lifecycle rules.
The application database transaction automatically rolls back the uploaded parts because the client never confirmed completion.
The CDN can serve the uploaded parts as a single object as long as their checksums are present.
questionData.question: In an S3-style multipart upload, the client successfully uploads every part but crashes before calling the completion endpoint. What is the correct system behavior to design for?

questions.explanation: Uploaded parts are not the same thing as a completed object. Until the completion call succeeds, blob storage has temporary multipart state that can cost money, so systems should use abort logic or lifecycle cleanup rules for abandoned uploads.

questions.question: For resumable uploads, a design that requires a distinct signed URL for each chunk is more S3-specific than provider-agnostic: S3 uses per-part presigned URLs, while GCS and Azure use a single resumable session URL with range-based chunk uploads.

questionData.question: For resumable uploads, a design that requires a distinct signed URL for each chunk is more S3-specific than provider-agnostic: S3 uses per-part presigned URLs, while GCS and Azure use a single resumable session URL with range-based chunk uploads.

questions.explanation: The article distinguishes S3 multipart uploads from GCS/Azure resumable uploads. The core capability is resumability, but the control-plane shape differs, so a portable design should abstract the upload session rather than hard-code S3’s per-part URL model.

questions.question: For a 100MB file that does not need SQL queries over its bytes, storing the file itself in the database is usually a poor tradeoff because it couples blob growth to database query performance, backups, and replication.

questionData.question: For a 100MB file that does not need SQL queries over its bytes, storing the file itself in the database is usually a poor tradeoff because it couples blob growth to database query performance, backups, and replication.

questions.explanation: The article argues that databases are suited for structured metadata, not large binary payloads. Keeping large files in object storage while storing metadata in the database lets storage scale independently and avoids making core database operations heavier.

questions.question: You support two private download workloads: popular 500MB training videos downloaded thousands of times worldwide, and rarely accessed compliance PDFs usually downloaded once by their owner. Based on the article's tradeoffs, which design is best?

options: Proxy both through application servers so authorization and bandwidth accounting stay centralized.
Use direct signed blob-storage URLs for the videos and signed CDN URLs for the PDFs.
Use signed CDN URLs for the popular videos, and direct signed blob-storage URLs for the rarely accessed PDFs.
Make both public blob-storage URLs because private files cannot benefit from CDN caching.
questionData.question: You support two private download workloads: popular 500MB training videos downloaded thousands of times worldwide, and rarely accessed compliance PDFs usually downloaded once by their owner. Based on the article's tradeoffs, which design is best?

questions.explanation: CDNs add cost and operational complexity but improve performance for frequently accessed files through geographic distribution and caching. For infrequent downloads, direct signed blob-storage URLs are simpler and cheaper while still preserving temporary access control.

questions.question: A private video is served through CloudFront using signed URLs. Which statement correctly describes how authorization is validated on each download request?

options: The CDN edge validates the signature using a public key, without calling your application server or origin for each request.
The CDN forwards every request to your application server, which checks the user's session before allowing the download.
S3 validates the CloudFront URL using your AWS secret access key, then tells the CDN whether to serve the file.
The browser exchanges the signed URL for temporary cloud credentials before downloading the object.
questionData.question: A private video is served through CloudFront using signed URLs. Which statement correctly describes how authorization is validated on each download request?

questions.explanation: CDN signed URLs are validated at the edge using public/private key cryptography: your server signs with the private key, and the CDN validates with the public key. This avoids putting your application server back in the request path for every download.
